options: A PL/SQL block with no name, compiled and run once, never saved as a database object
A stored procedure with a randomly generated name
A block that can only contain an EXCEPTION section
A package with no specification
questions.explain: It's a block run directly, with nothing permanent created — the rough PL/SQL equivalent of running a T-SQL batch ad hoc in SSMS.

questions.q: What is DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE roughly equivalent to in T-SQL?
options: PRINT
SELECT
TRY...CATCH
GO
questions.explain: Both are developer debugging tools for printing text output, not for returning real result sets.

questions.q: A block calls DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE with no error, but nothing appears on screen. What's the most likely cause?
options: SERVEROUTPUT was never turned on in the client tool
DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE can only be called inside a package
The block must have an EXCEPTION section for output to show
DBMS_OUTPUT only works inside named procedures, never anonymous blocks
questions.explain: DBMS_OUTPUT buffers its text; the client tool only displays it once SET SERVEROUTPUT ON has been run, typically once per session.

questions.q: Why doesn't T-SQL's PRINT have this same trip-up?
options: PRINT output always shows up in SSMS's Messages tab with no toggle needed first
T-SQL requires an even more complex setup than SET SERVEROUTPUT ON
PRINT and DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE behave identically, including the toggle requirement
T-SQL doesn't support printing text output at all
questions.explain: T-SQL has no equivalent setting to enable first, which is exactly why this step catches T-SQL developers off guard in Oracle.

questions.q: When would you reach for an anonymous block instead of a named stored procedure?
options: For ad hoc data fixes, one-time migrations, or quick debugging that doesn't need to be reusable
Whenever the logic needs to be called repeatedly by an application
Whenever the logic needs to be scheduled to run again later
Anonymous blocks should always be preferred over named procedures in production code
questions.explain: Reach for a named procedure once logic needs to be reusable or callable by other code; anonymous blocks are for one-off work.
